body: when it comes to regulating AI
. It’s merely a stand-in — a way to signal that you’re pushing against a future that no one wants.

On an economic level, AI is expected to decimate the workforce. The CEO of Anthropic, one of the largest AI companies, has warned that AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs. On a societal level, AI can be leveraged to promote misinformation and further undermine the public’s trust in democratic institutions. And on the civilizational level, AI presents major cybersecurity risks and poses threats to human life, especially as it becomes increasingly integrated in military decisions and weaponry.

So there’s a genuine interest in slowing down this technological advancement. And in the absence of robust federal regulations to fend off the worst possible outcomes, data centers make for a tangible target. They are starting to get more and more attention in elections across the country as candidates feel the need to address voters’ concerns about them. In an interview with the Globe’s editorial board, Graham Platner, a Democratic Senate candidate in Maine, floated the idea of regulating data centers like public utilities and potentially even making them publicly owned.

“There has never been a massive technological transformation that increases productivity that has ever done anything but disenfranchise and screw workers when left in the hands of corporate power,” Platner said. “I actually think one of the best ways that we can do this is by having the infrastructure that supports it like data centers — I very much think we should have some form of public ownership of those. … None of this runs without data centers.”

: With the Trump administration’s laissez-faire approach to AI, standing in the way of data center construction is one of the few routes states can take to tackle the broader regulatory problems around AI.

This regulation could come in various forms, including treating them like public utilities, taxing them in order to offset any potential increase in energy costs to consumers, and imposing requirements that would minimize their environmental risks

. And it’s especially important to put these sorts of regulations in place given that many states, despite all the local opposition, are competing to build data centers by offering tax breaks to companies instead of asking these multibillion-dollar corporations to pay their fair share when plugging into the grid.

Ultimately, it’s up to Congress to put up guardrails that will protect people from the risks posed by AI. And as long as the industry remains largely unregulated, nothing — not even a ban on the construction of new data centers — is stopping these corporations from abusing their power and using their technology in harmful and potentially dangerous ways.
